- Save game in the pause menu keeps the whole skirmish: every unit and building with its orders, health, stars and cargo, the money and build queues, the fog and what you remember under it, walls and gates, transports and their riders, superweapon charges, and the rival AI's plans.
- The game also saves itself every minute of play. The title screen offers Continue (the autosave) and Load saved game when there is one; loading puts you back exactly where you were, and the game plays on the same way it would have.
- Saves stay in your browser on this computer. A save from another version of the game is not offered (versions change the rules, so an old save could not play on the same way).

**Limitations:** One save slot plus the autosave. Control groups and the camera position are not saved.

versions.title: A cannier rival
versions.notes:
- On Normal and Hard the rival sells a building that is about to fall (under 15% and still being hit) for what it is still worth, never its only construction yard, and lines up the next building of its plan while one is under construction, so its base goes up without gaps.
- On Hard it also rebuilds what it lost: a destroyed or sold building goes back to the front of its plan.
- Its bombers pick targets in a new order: refineries first, then income buildings it has seen (Streaming Studio, Bake Sale, Fortune Stall), then power, then the rest. When you finish your first income building against a rival that uses bombers, a banner says so.
- AI against AI (balance table): Sparkle against the Council on Rocky Spine now falls at 313 to 351 s instead of 236 to 309 s, the Covenant now beats the Council on River Crossing too (305 to 361 s, these were draws), and the Sparkle mirror on River Crossing is decided near the end (399 and 419 s, both by the first start) instead of drawn.

**Limitations:** The rival still builds no walls and no transports. On Easy it does none of this.

versions.title: Ground patrol and hold
versions.notes:
- P then click now works for armed ground units too: they walk back and forth between where they stand and the click, fighting anything they meet on the way and then carrying on. Shift-click adds more points to the loop, as for fighters.
- G makes selected armed ground units hold position at once: they shoot whatever comes into range and never chase or step towards anything. Any other order ends it. Fighters keep G then click to guard a spot against aircraft.
- The sidebar shows P: patrol  G: hold for a selected trooper or tank, with (holding) or (on patrol).

**Limitations:** Harvesters and unarmed units ignore both orders. A holding unit still turns to face its target.

versions.title: Later tips
versions.notes:
- After the opening tips are done, the tip banner comes back once each for three moments: when your superweapon is first charged (how to aim it), when one of your buildings is first badly hurt (R repairs it), and when you are down to under 100 with nothing building (Z sells a building you can spare). Each stays up for eight seconds and never repeats in the same game.
- Switching tips off in Settings turns these off too.

**Limitations:** The later tips are the same words for every faction, with its superweapon and resource names filled in.

versions.title: Superweapons you aim
versions.notes:
- Superweapons land where you point them now. Press the button once it is charged and the cursor carries a ring; left-click on the map to fire, right-click or Esc to put it away. The ring is red over black fog: you cannot fire at a spot you have never seen.
- Each has its own size: the Encore heals and hastes your units within 9 tiles, the Pop Quiz stuns enemies within 7, the Night Parade frightens enemies within 6. Before, each touched every unit on the map.
- A ring marks the spot before it lands (1 s for the Encore, 2 s for the others), drawn for everyone who can see it, so a quick army can get out. The burst of confetti, exam papers or lanterns now fills the ring instead of the screen.
- The rival AI aims too: a blessing at the biggest knot of its own fighting units, a curse at the biggest knot of yours it can see. The balance table is unchanged (no AI superweapon lands before the twelve-game sets are decided).

**Limitations:** There is no on-screen countdown for the rival's ring beyond the ring itself.

versions.title: Infantry transports
versions.notes:
- Every faction has a flying transport on the Air tab: the Sparkle Tour Blimp (700), the Council Carpool Copter (750) and the Covenant Cloud Palanquin (650, from the Dojo once you have a Workshop). It is unarmed, needs no landing pad and carries five infantry.
- Select infantry and right-click one of your transports: they walk over and climb in (the ones that do not fit stay put). Fly it anywhere, over water and cliffs, and press U (or the Unload button) to drop everyone off on open ground below it.
- Riders keep who they are: their kills, their stars and their control group. Pressing a group's number while some of it is flying selects the transport they are in. Seat pips over the transport show how full it is, and the sidebar says Carrying 3 / 5.
- If a transport is shot down, everyone inside dies with it and the shooter gets every kill. Covenant riders still come back as ghosts.

**Limitations:** Only infantry can ride. The rival AI does not build transports yet, and there is no way to unload one rider at a time.

versions.title: Walls and gates
versions.notes:
- Every faction has a wall and a gate on the Def tab: the Merch Barricade and the VIP Entrance, the Umbrella Fence and the Late Slip Gate, the Prayer Slip Fence and the Moon Door. One tile each, no power, 100 and 300.
- Build a wall on the sidebar, then click where the row starts and drag: up to eight in a straight line. The first is the one you built; each extra segment is paid for as it goes down, and blocked tiles are skipped. The ghost shows the row, how many and what the extras cost.
- Your units walk through your own gates; everyone else is stopped at them. A unit attacking or attack-moving whose way is walled off breaks through the nearest wall or gate and carries on. Turrets and idle units never shoot walls on their own, walls give no build range, and a player with only walls left is beaten. R repairs walls and turrets like any building.
- Attack-move keeps going after a fight now. Before, a unit that stopped to shoot lost its path and stood still once the enemy died, so AI waves halted after their first skirmish. Waves push on to their goal, which makes the Sparkle rush stronger again on Rocky Spine; the Bass Dropper takes 6 s to train instead of 5 to make up some of it. Over twelve AI games, Sparkle beats the Council in six (earliest 236 s) and the Covenant in eight; River Crossing is mostly draws.

**Limitations:** The rival AI builds no walls yet. A gate does not open or close on screen; it just lets your side through.

versions.title: U deploys, rally lines, double-tap groups
versions.notes:
- U unfolds a mobile construction yard and packs a yard back up (the Deploy button still works). D only pans the camera now, so holding it never folds your base by accident.
- A selected barracks, factory or airfield draws a thick dashed line in your colour to its rally flag, and a selected refinery marks its dock (a ring where the harvesters unload) the same way.
- Tap a control group's number twice quickly (within a third of a second) to jump the camera to it, as well as selecting it. Shift still jumps on the first tap.

**Limitations:** The keys are fixed; there is no keymap screen yet.

versions.title: The Council catches up
versions.notes:
- Hall Monitors cost 125 Snacks instead of 150 and march a little faster (72 instead of 66), the Council's Hall Pass Checkpoint turret is tougher (816 hp instead of 680), and the Sparkle Bass Dropper costs 350 Hype instead of 300.
- AI against AI on Rocky Spine, Sparkle against Council in both seatings: before, the Council fell at 237 to 247 s with 15 to 18 kills to Sparkle's 28; now it falls at 281 to 299 s with 18 to 22 kills to 25 or 26, and on River Crossing three of four games are draws (Sparkle won one at 367 s). Over twelve games with three different starting purses, Sparkle's earliest win moved from 211 s to 281 s and the Council's kills at 300 s went from behind (189 to 229) to ahead (321 to 350).
- The Covenant still beats the Council on Rocky Spine (274 to 359 s, as before), and on River Crossing the four games are draws now instead of Covenant wins.

**Limitations:** Sparkle still beats the Council on Rocky Spine, about a minute later than before. Twenty-percent changes to unit costs and buildings could not close it: the Council's army trades evenly in the first clash, but Sparkle refills faster and its Bass Droppers then take the base apart.

versions.title: Both seats get the same start
versions.notes:
- On Rocky Spine the bottom-left start used to land one more harvester trip by 100 s than the top-right one (deposits at 100 s in the AI mirror matches: Sparkle 5000 against 4500, Council 4800 against 4200, Covenant 4950 against 4400). Now both seats deposit exactly the same (5000 / 5000, 4800 / 4800, 4950 / 4950) until the armies meet.
- The cause was three tie-breaks that did not turn with the seat: which ore tile a harvester picks next when two are equally near (one seat walked up its pile toward the refinery, the other sideways away from it), which tile units leave a building from when its middle sits on a tile edge, and the order units take their turn in (the first seat always shot first). All three are mirrored or alternate now, and pathing and the separation push no longer depend on order either.
- The fights that follow are closer: kills at 200 s in the Rocky Spine mirror matches went from 21 / 30 to 28 / 30 (Sparkle) and from 18 / 13 to 18 / 15 (Council). River Crossing was already even and stays so.

**Limitations:** The Council mirror on Rocky Spine is still won by the bottom-left start, late (387 s), from either seating; once the first armies clash, tiny rounding differences grow and decide close games.

versions.title: A cleaner title screen
versions.notes:
- You and Rival are drop-downs now, with each faction's one-line blurb under them; the rival's difficulty is a drop-down too and the fog of war is a toggle. Tab, the arrows and Enter work through all of it.
- Map opens its own screen: the maps on the left, a drawn preview of the highlighted one on the right (terrain, the gold resource fields, a white marker on each start with yours in pink) with its size and player count, and Back and Select below. Enter on a map selects it.
- Menu buttons keep their width whatever sits above them.

**Limitations:** The preview is the map at four pixels a tile; it does not show where the rival will build.

versions.title: The mobile construction yard
versions.notes:
- A mobile construction yard for every faction from the war factory, once you have a refinery: the Tour Bus, the Committee Van and the Portable Shrine. Dear, slow, unarmed and tough. Drive it somewhere with room, press D or the sidebar's Deploy button, and it unfolds into a second construction yard; the footprint is shown under it, green when it fits and red with the reason when it does not.
- A second yard lets you build out there, and construction runs half again as fast while you own two (twice as fast with three or more). D (or Pack up) folds any construction yard back into its vehicle, the first one included.
- You are not beaten while you still have a mobile yard rolling, even with every building gone.
- The Hard rival buys one once its home field runs low, drives it to a free footprint by the nearest field that still has ore, and unfolds it there; its next refinery goes up beside the new yard.

**Limitations:** D also pans the camera right, so a tap nudges the view a little; hold WASD with nothing deployable selected. The rival never packs a yard up again.

versions.title: Have a good look at the enemy
versions.notes:
- Click an enemy unit or building (or drag a box with only enemies in it) to look at it: a red ring, its health bar, and the sidebar tells you its name, faction, armour, weapon and range, hit points, and for a building what it trains and its power. You cannot give it orders, and the number keys will not group it.
- Hover over any enemy you can see for a moment and a small name-and-hp tip appears by the cursor.
- Under the fog you can only look at what you can see, plus the buildings you remember: a remembered one shows its last-seen health until somebody looks again.
- Your own units' panel got the same armour, weapon and range line.

**Limitations:** A look at several enemies only counts them by type; a remembered building shows a percentage, not exact hit points.

versions.title: Three stars, and the third one heals
versions.notes:
- Veterancy has three ranks now: one star at 3 kills, two at 8, three at 15, for +25%, +50% and +75% damage. The stars line up by the health bar, the promotion shout gets bigger with each rank, and each rank has its own lines (the Council minutes its second star; the Covenant becomes a minor deity, very minor).
- A three-star unit patches itself up: 1% of its health a second whenever it has not been hit for three seconds. Ghosts fade anyway and buildings have Repair, so neither does.
- The sidebar says the rank and the bonus for a selected veteran (Kills 9, 2-star, +50% damage).

**Limitations:** Kills from splash and from conversions count the same as any other; a unit never loses a star.

versions.title: You can see the Cheer now
versions.notes:
- The Center's cheer radius is drawn as a ring: faint all the time, bright with sparkles running round it while the Center or anyone it is cheering is selected.
- Every unit firing faster inside the ring wears a little pink musical note by its health bar, and its muzzle flash is bigger and pinker, so you can see who is on the beat at a glance.
- The sidebar says what the aura does: the Center's button tooltip and its info box read Cheer: +50% fire rate for friends within 4 tiles. Any future unit with an aura gets all of this from its data.

**Limitations:** Only armed units are counted as cheered; a harvester in the ring hums along for free.

versions.title: Primary buildings and rally flags
versions.notes:
- With several barracks, factories or airfields, one of each kind is the primary and that is where the units you build on the sidebar come out, so a forward factory can feed the front. The first one you build is the primary; select another and press Y or the sidebar's Primary button to switch. It wears a gold star, on the map and on the minimap, and the sidebar tab's tooltip names it.
- When the primary falls, the oldest one left takes over by itself.
- Every producing building keeps its own rally flag: select it and right-click to plant the flag; it is drawn while the building is selected. An airfield's flag is where its new fighters go and circle on guard; leave it alone and they park on the pads as before.
- The Covenant's Dojo trains infantry and spirits, so one Dojo is the primary for both.

**Limitations:** The rival keeps one building of each kind and does not pick primaries. A bomber ignores the airfield flag; it has nowhere to circle.

versions.title: The repair bay
versions.notes:
- A repair bay for every faction, on the Def tab once you have a barracks: the Green Room, the Nurse's Office and the Hot Spring. Every friendly infantry unit and vehicle within five tiles heals 3% of its health a second, half that while you are low on power. Aircraft have their pads and buildings have Repair, so neither is touched.
- The heal radius is drawn as a soft green ring while the bay is selected or being placed, and a unit being patched up wears a bobbing green plus.
- The rival builds its bay right after its war factory, and sends badly hurt units home to it.

**Limitations:** The ring heals through walls and fog; a bay never moves.

versions.title: Control groups you can see
versions.notes:
- Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+9 saves the selected units as that group and says so (Group 3: 5 units); the number alone selects them again, Shift and the number jumps the camera to them too.
- Every grouped unit wears its number in a little tag by its health bar, and the sidebar has a strip of the nine groups with how many units are in each: click one to select it.
- After a tab key (B, E, I, V, F) the numbers build for three seconds as before, but a click on the map ends that at once, and a number with no button behind it picks the group instead, so a recall is never swallowed.
- The fourth tutorial tip mentions the groups.

**Limitations:** A unit is in one group at a time; buildings cannot be grouped.

versions.title: Fighters on patrol and on guard
versions.notes:
- Guard: select fighters (Wing Idol, Paper Plane, Will-o-Wisp), press G and click, or just right-click a spot. They fly there, hover, and shoot down any enemy aircraft that comes within their sight; out of missiles they go home to rearm and come straight back to the post.
- Patrol: P then click flies a loop from where they are to the point and back; Shift-click adds more points. On patrol they attack enemy aircraft and anything on the ground they can hit, then carry on round the loop, rearming when they must.
- The guard ring and the patrol loop are drawn while the fighters are selected; the sidebar shows what a selected fighter is doing.
- The rival puts its idle fighters on guard over its base once it has seen your aircraft.
- The sidebar's selection box keeps to four lines whatever is selected, so the panel always fits a 720p window.

**Limitations:** A guard only minds the air; a patrol stops for ground targets too. Bombers cannot patrol or guard.

versions.title: Radar and scouts
versions.notes:
- A Radar building for every faction, on the Base tab once you have a refinery: the Fan Mail Dish, the AV Club Antenna and the Omen Bell. While powered it sweeps every ten seconds, and every enemy unit standing in your grey fog shows as a fading blip on the map and the minimap for ten seconds. Blips are rumours, not targets: send a spotter.
- A scout unit for every faction: the Street Team Scooter and the Hall Monitor Bike from the war factory, the Lantern Spirit from the Dojo. Unarmed, very fast, sees for miles.
- The rival builds its radar right after its refinery on Normal and Hard, buys a scout unit when it has none, and sends that instead of an infantry squad.

**Limitations:** Blips are where the unit stood at the sweep; they do not follow it. With fog of war off the radar sweeps for nothing.

versions.title: Artillery fires into grey, never into black
versions.notes:
- Under fog of war, artillery (and anything else whose range is longer than its sight) can only fire at what you can see right now, or at enemy buildings you have seen before, which stay on the map in the grey fog. It will not fire at units hidden in fog, nor at anything in the black, and it will not pick such targets on its own either. Ordered at something it cannot see, it drives closer until it can.
- Enemy buildings you have seen are remembered as last seen. If one is destroyed while nobody of yours is looking, it stays as a greyed ghost with a question mark on the map and the minimap until a friendly looks at the tile; right-click the ghost to shell the spot anyway.
- The cursor says NOT SCOUTED over the black with units selected, so you know why nothing there can be targeted.
- With fog of war off, nothing changes.

**Limitations:** No radar yet: units in the grey fog are invisible until a spotter sees them. The Radar building and a scout unit per faction come in the next release.

versions.title: Harvesters stay home
versions.notes:
- A harvester whose pile runs out no longer drives across the map to the next field. It keeps to its own pile while any of it is left, then to a field within eight tiles of its refinery, and otherwise it delivers what it has, parks beside the refinery, says so ('Pile's empty, boss!') and waits.
- A parked harvester looks again every five seconds, so it goes back to work by itself when its pile sprouts again.
- Right-click a field to send it anywhere you like; that order may go as far as it wants.
- The rival keeps its own targeting and sends its waiting harvesters to whatever field still has something.

**Limitations:** A harvester that has never mined (a new one, or one that just changed sides) still picks the nearest field anywhere for its first trip.

versions.title: The income floor
versions.notes:
- You can no longer be stuck with nothing: a finished construction yard pays 3 a second, power or not, shown as +3/s at the right of the money row. With no harvester and less than the price of one, the sidebar says so and the readout turns yellow.
- Empty field tiles sprout again after three minutes at half their amount and grow back one a second, so long games do not starve.
- An investment building for every faction, from the Base tab once you have a refinery: the Streaming Studio, the Bake Sale and the Fortune Stall. 2000 each, +6 a second while powered (about six minutes to pay off), as many as you like, flimsy on purpose. The rival builds one on Normal and two on Hard once it has two harvesters and money to spare.
- The sidebar has a Def tab (E) for the turret and the anti-air tower, so the Base tab keeps to four rows.

**Limitations:** The income readout counts the local player's buildings only; the rival's investments are not shown.

versions.title: Bombers meet anti-air
versions.notes:
- Anti-air is the counter again. Bombers have less health (Confetti Bomber 280 to 220, Field Trip Bus 380 to 300, Umbrella Ghost 230 to 200) and anti-air towers hit much harder: a Speaker Tower volley does 108 to aircraft instead of 48, a Fire Drill Siren 120 instead of 56, a Wind Chime 108 instead of 50. A bomber now dies to three tower volleys (two for the Umbrella Ghost) where it took five to seven.
- Rockets do 20% more to aircraft, so a Bass Dropper drops a Confetti Bomber in three shots instead of four. Bombs barely scratch infantry (a Bass Dropper survives a direct hit with 6 hp; a Fan Girl does not), so anti-air infantry can stand under a raid.
- Bombers drop one bomb per pass: after a drop they overshoot and come round again, and the second bomb lands a few seconds later. Reloading on the pad takes five seconds a bomb instead of one and a half.
- An anti-air truck for every faction, from the war factory: the Confetti Flak (650), the Hall Pass Flak (700) and the Wind Chime Wagon (620). Light armour, flak that reaches aircraft at 260 px and nothing on the ground; one beats a bomber one on one and loses to any tank. The rival builds one or two once it has seen your aircraft.

**Limitations:** Fighters (Wing Idol, Paper Plane, Will-o-Wisp) are untouched, but the harder towers now shoot them down in two volleys too; keep them away from the base defences.

versions.title: Queued orders
versions.notes:
- Hold Shift when you right-click and the order waits behind what the unit is doing: move, attack, attack-move (Shift + Q click, or Shift + Ctrl + right-click), harvest, return and send-planes-home all queue, up to eight deep.
- Selected units with orders waiting show their route as a dashed line through the waypoints (red for attacks).
- X clears the queue along with the current order; a plain order and a transform clear it too; a unit that changes sides forgets it.
- The hotkey strip and the pause menu mention it.

**Limitations:** A harvest order in the middle of a queue never ends on its own (harvesters keep harvesting), so put it last. The AI does not queue.

versions.title: The far right of the map
versions.notes:
- The sidebar no longer hides the last columns of the map: the camera can scroll far enough right (and down, past the hotkey strip) that every tile shows in the open part of the screen, at every zoom.
- The minimap's view rectangle shows the part of the map you can actually see, not what the sidebar covers, and a click near the minimap's edge looks right at that edge.

**Limitations:** The map's top and left edges still stop at the screen edge, as before; only the sides the HUD covers scroll further.

versions.title: Haunt
versions.notes:
- The Covenant's gimmick. Every Covenant fighter (not the Ox Cart, not the spirits) comes back once as a Restless Ghost where it fell: a weak floating wail that goes for its killer and fades after twenty seconds.
- Fox Priestess: a new Covenant infantry unit (two at a time). Her Curse reaches aircraft, and any enemy unit left under 35% health by it changes sides on the spot, keeping its health, kills and star.
- A cursed harvester goes to work for its new owner, a cursed aircraft leaves its pad and looks for one of yours, and a cursed unit drops out of your selection and control groups.
- A conversion counts as a kill for the Fox Priestess, so three curses make her a veteran.
- The sidebar says 'an Offering Box' instead of 'a Offering Box'.

**Limitations:** Ghosts do not come back for the rival's cursed units until those die as Covenant units (then they do). Buildings cannot be cursed.

versions.title: The Yokai Shrine Covenant
versions.notes:
- A third faction, picked on the title screen for you or the rival: the Yokai Shrine Covenant, a cursed shrine whose spirits unionised. Deep purple and lantern orange, and everything is slightly damp.
- Offerings are collected from Offering Piles (coins, rice balls, the odd apple) by an Ox Cart whose ox is also a ghost.
- Buildings: Torii Gate, Haunted Lantern, Offering Box, Dojo, Kiln, Komainu Statue, Wind Chime, and the Haunted Well.
- Infantry: Shrine Maiden (paper charms, cheap), Kappa (cucumber launcher, anti-vehicle and anti-air, slow on land), Oni (heavy, iron club, walks up to things).
- Vehicles: Rolling Lantern (a fire-breathing tank), Thunder Drum (artillery), Ox Cart.
- No airfield: the Will-o-Wisp and the Umbrella Ghost float straight out of the Dojo, park nowhere and never reload.
- Superweapon: the Night Parade. Every enemy unit loses a quarter of its health to fright (never the last point) and freezes for three seconds, under a sky of rising lanterns.
- The rival AI plays the Covenant on every difficulty from the data table alone.

**Limitations:** The Haunt gimmick (dead units returning as ghosts, and the Fox Priestess whose curse converts a weak enemy) comes in the next release.

versions.title: Veterans and nervous harvesters
versions.notes:
- Veterancy: a unit that gets three kills earns a gold star, does 25% more damage, and shouts in a much bigger bubble. The star survives a transform.
- Select a unit to see its kills.
- Harvesters under fire stop harvesting and run for your nearest building (a turret, if one is close), shouting about it. Eight seconds later they go back to work on their own.
- A harvester you have ordered to move, or one that is transforming, keeps to its order.

**Limitations:** Buildings and their turrets do not earn stars. There is only one rank.

versions.title: Tips and silly deaths
versions.notes:
- A tutorial banner for the first two minutes: build power, then a refinery, then a barracks, train six fighters, and brace for the first attack. Each faction words it its own way (the Student Council numbers its agenda items).
- Tutorial tips can be switched off in Settings.
- Infantry no longer fall over: they are flung off the top of the screen, spinning, trailing their faction's death cry one letter at a time (NOOOOOO, or OBJECTION).
- Vehicles pop into confetti and one wheel rolls away. Aircraft spiral off with a whistle and a trail of smoke.
- Buildings come down in chunks, and the screen shakes if you are watching.

**Limitations:** The banner covers the opening only; there is no tip for superweapons, repair or selling yet.

versions.title: Repair, Sell and a build queue
versions.notes:
- Repair: press R (or the Repair button), then click damaged buildings. A building under repair shows a green plus, heals over 25 seconds and costs up to 40% of its price. No money, no repair crew.
- Sell: press Z or Delete (or the Sell button), then click a building. You get half its price, less if it is damaged, plus a refund for anything it was training. You cannot sell your last building.
- Build queue: click buildings while one is under construction and up to five wait in line. Each is paid for when its turn comes. Right-click a button to take one off the queue.
- Sidebar hotkeys: B, I, V and F open the Base, Infantry, Vehicles and Aircraft tabs, and for the next three seconds the number keys press that tab's buttons (B then 2 builds the second building; I then 1 1 1 trains three).
- Repair and Sell stay on until you right-click, and the cursor says which mode it is in.
- The rival AI repairs its buildings on Normal and Hard.

**Limitations:** The number keys are control groups unless a tab key was pressed in the last three seconds.

versions.title: Easy, Normal, Hard
versions.notes:
- Rival AI difficulty on the title screen, remembered: Easy, Normal or Hard.
- Easy: it thinks slowly, starts with less, keeps a small army, attacks after five minutes and leaves its superweapon alone.
- Normal and Hard now play under the same fog of war as you. They start knowing nothing, send a scout to find your base, and only attack buildings they have seen. Turn the fog off and they see everything again.
- Hard starts with extra money, runs three harvesters per refinery, and attacks sooner and more often.
- On Normal and Hard, bombers go for your refineries instead of flying with the attack waves.

**Limitations:** The scout is not coming home. Easy still sees the whole map; it just does very little with it.

versions.title: Superweapons
versions.notes:
- Encore (Sparkle Dominion): build an Encore Stage. After four minutes of charge, press the button and your whole army heals to full and fires twice as fast for ten seconds, under a screen full of confetti.
- Pop Quiz (Student Council): build an Exam Hall. After four minutes, every enemy unit stops for five seconds to fill in a form. Exam papers rain from the sky. Nobody studied.
- Both superweapons show a charge timer on the sidebar: yours as a bar that turns into the fire button, the rival's in red. You are warned 30 seconds before the rival's is ready, when it is ready, and when it goes off.
- Low power pauses the charge. Losing the building loses the charge.
- The rival AI builds its own superweapon and saves it for a real fight.
- Debug: Ctrl+Shift+F9 gives both sides a superweapon building, yours charged, to try the effects.

**Limitations:** Superweapons hit the whole map; there is no targeting. Defence buildings ignore the Pop Quiz.

versions.title: Fair starts and readable buttons
versions.notes:
- The resource field is drawn the way your faction sees it: Hype Crystals for the Sparkle Dominion, wrapped Rock Candy for the Student Council. Same field, same amounts.
- Sidebar build buttons wrap long names onto two lines instead of cutting them off (Hall Pass Checkpoint, Club Budget Reactor, Fire Drill Siren). The third line is the cost, or the progress, READY, or how many are queued.
- Rocky Spine is now the same ground for both bases, rotated half a turn, like River Crossing. The top-right base moved two tiles.
- The rival AI builds its refinery next to its field from either start. Before, only the top-right AI got a short harvest run, and it won every AI-vs-AI game inside 200 seconds.
- Refineries dock harvesters on the side that faces the field. Units ordered onto a building stop on the side they came from.

**Limitations:** In AI-vs-AI the Sparkle Dominion still beats the Student Council from either start: that is balance, not the map.

versions.title: River Crossing
versions.notes:
- A second map, River Crossing: a river runs down the middle with three bridges, bases on the left and right, a crystal field behind each base and one at the far end of the top and bottom bridges. Both sides get the same ground, rotated.
- Map picker on the title screen (Rocky Spine or River Crossing), remembered.
- Aircraft ignore the river; everyone else has to hold a bridge.

**Limitations:** Two maps, two players each. No naval units, so the river is only an obstacle.

versions.title: Fog of war
versions.notes:
- Fog of war: the map starts black. Your units and buildings reveal what is within their sight range; ground you have left stays on the map, dimmed.
- Enemy units only show while one of yours can see them. Enemy buildings stay on the map once you have seen them. Shots, shouts and explosions in the fog are neither drawn nor heard.
- The minimap follows the same rules, and you cannot click or target what the fog hides.
- A blinded unit (hit by the Student Council's Projector Cannon) sees half as far.
- Fog of war: On / Off on the title screen, remembered. The rival AI plays with full knowledge either way.

**Limitations:** A destroyed enemy building disappears from the map even if you were not looking. The AI does not scout; it always knows where you are.

versions.title: Defence buildings
versions.notes:
- Each faction gets two defence buildings on the Base tab, both needing a barracks: the Sparkle Dominion builds the Glowstick Turret (anti-ground) and the Speaker Tower (anti-air); the Student Council builds the Hall Pass Checkpoint and the Fire Drill Siren.
- Defences shoot whatever comes into range, with a barrel that follows the target. They draw power, and go offline when your base is low on power.
- Attackers go for buildings that shoot back before the rest of a base.
- The AI builds an anti-ground and an anti-air defence, then a second turret, on the side of its base that faces the middle of the map.
- Fixed: a building that was hit stayed flashed white.

**Limitations:** Defences cannot be repaired or sold yet. Turrets have no upgrade path.

versions.title: Student Council of Steel
versions.notes:
- A second faction: the Student Council of Steel, a school council that spent the entire budget on mecha. Navy and white, Snacks instead of Hype (harvested from the same crystals, which they insist are Rock Candy), and deadpan announcements.
- Buildings: Council Office, Club Budget Reactor, Cafeteria, Homeroom, Robotics Club, Rooftop.
- Infantry: Hall Monitor, Treasurer (a sniper whose every shot costs 15 Snacks), Vice President (a hero mech, one at a time).
- Every Council vehicle has a second mode. Select it and press T: the Lunch Truck stands up into an armed Lunch Walker, the Desk Walker becomes a Standing Desk with anti-air missiles, and the Projector Cannon deploys into artillery that blinds what it hits (blinded units see and shoot half as far). A deployed projector packs itself up when you tell it to move.
- Aircraft: Paper Plane (fighter) and Field Trip Bus (bomber).
- Faction picker on the title screen: choose your faction and your rival's. The choice is remembered.
- The AI plays either faction, and decides by itself when its vehicles should transform.

**Limitations:** Aircraft do not transform yet. The Field Trip Bus is a bomber until transports exist. The Council's economy is slower by design; in AI hands it is a little weaker than the Sparkle Dominion.

versions.title: Factions are data
versions.notes:
- Nothing in the game engine names a faction any more: the resource name, the name of the crystal fields, starting units, the AI's build order and army, win and lose lines, the sidebar tip and the sidebar colour all come from the faction table. This is the groundwork for the second faction.
- Team colours come from the faction (a mirror match gives the second player the faction's second colour).
- The bottom strip also shows how long one simulation step takes (sim ms), which stays meaningful when the browser tab is in the background.
- A headless AI-versus-AI game is part of the smoke test.

**Limitations:** Still one faction. No visible changes to play.

versions.title: Sound and feel
versions.notes:
- Procedural sound: glowstick pews, bass shells, rockets, sparkles, confetti bombs, booms and kabooms, dings when things finish, coins when Hype lands, a cheer when you place a building, a pop for every shout.
- Infantry bob as they walk, aircraft hover, muzzle flashes, flowers in the grass.
- The pause menu lists every control. The bottom strip shows fps and unit count.
- Ctrl+Shift+F8 starts a 160-unit brawl in the middle of the map, for performance checks.

**Limitations:** Sounds are synthesized bleeps, not voice acting. Music later.

versions.title: Skirmish AI, win and lose, minimap
versions.notes:
- The blue Sparkle Dominion builds a base, harvests, trains a mixed army, defends its base, and sends waves (first around 3 minutes, then every 100 s or whenever 10 units are idle).
- Win by flattening every blue building; lose when you have none left. The end screen shows time, kills, losses and Hype.
- Minimap in the sidebar: terrain, Hype fields, every unit and building, the camera box. Left-click to look, right-click to move the selection.

**Limitations:** The AI plays one difficulty and one faction. No fog of war. Aircraft and artillery are cheap on the sidebar but the AI rarely uses the bomber.

versions.title: Aircraft
versions.notes:
- Sky Stage has four pads; new Wing Idols and Confetti Bombers appear parked on them (no free pad, no more planes).
- Aircraft fire their ammo, fly home, reload one shot every 1.5 s and resume the attack. Idle planes return to their pad.
- Right-click your Sky Stage with planes selected to send them home. Selected planes show their ammo pips.
- Bass Droppers and Wing Idols shoot at aircraft; tanks and Fan Girls can't.

**Limitations:** No enemy AI yet: the blue base just sits there. Planes without a Sky Stage hover where they are.

versions.title: Combat, infantry and vehicles
versions.notes:
- Weapons and the armour matrix: glowsticks shred infantry, speaker bazookas pop tanks and aircraft, glitter cannons squash infantry, bass shells splash.
- Right-click an enemy to attack; Q then click to attack-move; idle units shoot what comes close and fight back when hit.
- The Center's cheer: nearby friends fire 50% faster. Bass Cannons hold fire inside their minimum range.
- Tracers, hit flashes, death pops, x_x and KABOOM, dying shouts.

**Limitations:** Aircraft fire their ammo and then stop: rearming lands in v0.1.4. No enemy AI yet.

versions.title: Economy and base building
versions.notes:
- Sidebar on the right: Hype, power bar, Base / Inf / Veh / Air tabs with build buttons, progress and queue counts.
- Red Alert construction: build from the sidebar, click READY, place next to your base (green ghost = ok). Right-click a button to cancel.
- Glowstick Generator, Merch Booth (comes with a Fan Van), Idol Academy, Stage Garage, Sky Stage; prerequisites and a one-Center limit.
- Fan Vans harvest Hype Crystals and haul 500 Hype back to the nearest Merch Booth, then go back for more. Fields deplete.
- Power: buildings draw it, generators make it; a deficit halves build and training speed.

**Limitations:** No combat yet: units can be trained and moved but nothing fights. Aircraft do not rearm.

versions.title: Sim core: map, camera, selection, orders
versions.notes:
- A 64x48 skirmish map with rocks, water and Hype Crystal fields; pink base bottom-left, blue base top-right.
- Chibi Fan Girls and Glitter Tanks with team colours, selection rings, health bars and shout bubbles.
- Drag-box and click selection, double-click for same type, Shift to add; right-click move; Q attack-move; X stop; Ctrl+1-9 control groups.
- Grid pathing around rocks and buildings with local avoidance; aircraft fly straight.
- Camera: WASD / arrows / screen edges pan, mouse wheel zooms.

**Limitations:** No economy, production or combat yet; units can be ordered around but nothing fights.

versions.title: First playable
versions.notes: - Title screen, pause menu (Esc or Tab), settings, and this version log.

versions.title: Polish
versions.notes:
- How-to tips under the first lots, hidden once you make a move.
- Menus sit on rounded panels and buttons have their own colours, so text is easier to read over the lot.
- Smaller HUD on narrow phone screens so every button fits.
- The win panel names the lot you cleared.

versions.title: Juice and sound
versions.notes:
- Sounds made in code: slide, bump, pick, button click, engine vroom, win jingle and a chime per star.
- Slides ease in with a little overshoot; pushing a vehicle into something thumps and shakes it.
- When your car gets out, the barrier arm lifts, the car backs up a touch and floors it, and confetti flies.
- Stars pop in one by one on the win panel. Car colours no longer look like buses.

versions.title: Forty lots
versions.notes:
- 40 lots: 30 on 6x6 lots ramping from 2 to 30 moves, then 10 bigger 7x7 lots with planters in the way.
- Every lot is made by a generator and checked by the solver, so par is the true fewest moves.
- Choose lot screen with 1 to 3 stars per lot; lots open as you clear the one before.
- Best moves saved per lot and shown on the HUD; the win panel shows your stars and a new best.

**Limitations:** No sound yet.

versions.title: Core puzzle
versions.notes:
- A 6x6 parking lot in 3D: slide cars and buses along their lanes to clear a way for your red car.
- Drag vehicles with the mouse or a finger; or pick one with a click or Space and slide it with the arrow keys or WASD.
- Move counter (sliding the same vehicle again counts once), undo (Z), restart (R) and par for each lot.
- Three lots to clear, each checked by a solver.

**Limitations:** Only three lots and no sound yet.

versions.title: First playable
versions.notes: - Title screen, pause menu (Esc or Tab), settings, and this version log.

versions.title: Edit orders from the map
versions.notes:
- Click an order arrow on the map to pick it: it lights up with its row, and a small box by the arrow lets you change how many troops go (-1, +1, All or a slider) or delete it. Click elsewhere or press Esc to close it.
- Every deploy and move in the order list has its own -1 and +1 buttons. A move can't send more than its region holds (one always stays behind); a deploy can't use more troops than you have left.
- Click an order in the list to light up its arrow. Arrows between the same two regions in opposite directions no longer sit on top of each other.

versions.title: End orders, always in reach
versions.notes:
- End orders and Clear sit in a bar pinned to the bottom of the sidebar, so you never scroll to find them. Online it shows Waiting for others once your orders are in.
- Ending your turn asks once: End turn or Keep editing. With troops still to place, that same dialog warns you instead. Enter opens it and Enter again answers it.
- Settings: turn off the end-turn confirm (the troops-left warning still shows).
- Clear can be undone.

versions.title: Deploy mode
versions.notes:
- Orders now have two modes: Deploy (D) and Move / Attack (M). Each turn opens in Deploy while you have troops to place.
- In Deploy mode, tap your regions to place troops one at a time (shift-click places 5). Right-click or long-press takes one back; -1, +5 and All here buttons work on the region you last tapped.
- Once every troop is placed the game switches to Move / Attack by itself; switch back any time.

versions.title: Tidier sidebar, no forgotten troops
versions.notes:
- Sidebar sections (Players, Orders, Truces, Battle log) open and close from their headers, and stay how you left them. Truces start closed; a closed header still shows its count, and a waiting truce offer lights it up.
- Ending your orders with troops still to deploy asks first: Deploy them, or End anyway. Settings can make it a hard rule instead.
- The reinforcements line is highlighted while any are left.
- Online: when the turn timer runs out, troops you didn't place go to your region with the most enemies next to it.

versions.title: Pick your start
versions.notes:
- New game: each human player picks where they start, from a list or by clicking a numbered start on the map preview. Auto keeps your usual start; Random draws one when the game begins.
- Two players can't take the same start. AI players keep theirs unless someone took it, then get a free one decided by the seed.
- Online: everyone in the lobby picks their own start and sees the map; the host's game settles any clash before the game begins.

versions.title: Map previews
versions.notes:
- New game (and the online lobby) shows a drawn preview of the chosen map: its regions, borders and links, each starting region in its player's colour and neutral land in grey.
- The preview follows the map and player count you pick, and works for maps you made in the editor too.

versions.title: Rooms that stay open
versions.notes:
- Online: the host keeps its room alive while everyone thinks, so a player who refreshes after a long pause can still rejoin.
- If the host loses the signaling server mid-game (it restarts or the network drops), the game carries on and the host reopens the same room code by itself.

versions.title: Fairer seats on The Ring
versions.notes:
- AI players break ties between equally good targets with the game seed instead of map order. On The Ring, Pinecrest (seat 6) used to win about a third of all-AI games; now every seat wins about a sixth.
- All-AI games with Deterministic battles now play out differently for each seed (before, equal AIs played the same game every time).

versions.title: Hotseat fog
versions.notes:
- Fog of war with two or more players at one screen: while a turn plays out, the board shows only what every one of you can see, so nobody learns anything from the shared screen.
- After the pass-the-device screen, each player gets a private Last turn report of everything they saw happen. Reopen it with Last turn report in your orders.

**Limitations:** The report is not kept in saves: loading a game mid-turn starts without one.

versions.title: Sound
versions.notes:
- Sound effects, made in code: order clicks, deploys, marching armies, battle clashes, captures and held regions, commanders captured or fallen.
- Chimes for truce offers and truces, a warning when a rival is about to win on the goal, a ticking clock in the last 10 seconds of an online turn, and win and defeat stings.
- Nothing plays for battles hidden by fog or while skipping. The Volume setting controls it.

**Limitations:** Browsers start sound only after your first click.

versions.title: Capture the Heart
versions.notes:
- Maps can have goal regions (marked GOAL). Hold every one of them at the end of enough turns in a row and you win.
- The Ring now has a goal: hold The Heart for 5 turns in a row. New game option Map goal (on by default where a map has one).
- The side panel shows who holds the goal and for how long; it turns red when a rival is close.
- Map editor: tick Goal region on any region, and set how many turns it must be held.
- AI players go after the goal and after a rival who holds it.

versions.title: Map scenarios
versions.notes:
- Maps can suggest scenario settings: a start bonus (extra reinforcements for everyone on turn 1) and a turn limit. Set them in the map editor's Scenario block.
- Picking a map in New game fills in its presets; you can still change them. New option: Start bonus.
- Twin Isles now starts with +5 reinforcements; Crossroads suggests a 30-turn limit.

versions.title: Replays
versions.notes:
- Every game now records its orders. When it ends, Watch replay on the win screen plays it again from turn 1, with fog lifted.
- Replay controls: Next, Prev, Play / Pause, Speed, Skip and Exit replay.
- Saves and exported codes keep the replay, so a finished game loaded later (or on another device) can be watched too.

**Limitations:** Games started before this version have no replay.

versions.title: Online turn timer
versions.notes:
- Online games can have a turn timer (45 seconds, 90 seconds or 3 minutes), set by the host in the lobby.
- The clock shows in the side panel and turns red in the last 15 seconds. It starts once everyone has watched the last turn.
- When time runs out, the orders you have so far are sent. A player who sent nothing gives no orders that turn.

versions.title: Rejoin online games
versions.notes:
- Refresh the page (or lose the connection) during an online game and you get your seat back: the host sends you the game as it stands.
- Closed the tab? Join the same room with the same name to take back a seat the AI was playing.
- The room code is kept in the address bar, so a refresh rejoins on its own.
- Players on a different game version are told to reload instead of joining.

**Limitations:** If the host leaves, the online game ends (it can be played on locally).

versions.title: Truces
versions.notes:
- Offer another player a truce for 3, 5 or 10 turns from the Truces block in your orders. When both sides agree, attacks between you fail until it ends.
- Offers are revealed with the other orders and stay open through the next turn; accepting starts the truce before anyone moves that turn.
- AI players accept truces from real rivals, sometimes offer them to their biggest neighbour, and never attack a partner.
- Truces need three or more players: when only two are left, they end. New game option to turn truces off.

versions.title: Fog of war
versions.notes:
- New game option: Fog of war. You see armies only in your regions and their neighbours; the rest show "?". Who owns what stays visible.
- During the reveal you only see orders and battles near your land. Other players' army totals are hidden.
- The AI plays by the same rule: it plans only on what it can see.

**Limitations:** Several players on one device share a screen, so while a turn plays out the board shows what any of them can see.

versions.title: Three new maps
versions.notes:
- New maps: Twin Isles (2 players), Crossroads (4 players) and The Ring (6 players).
- Each marks where commanders start; open them in the map editor to make your own versions.

versions.title: Map editor
versions.notes:
- Map editor on the title screen: place regions and sea points, link neighbours (or auto-link touching ones), set names, starting owners, armies, income and commander starts.
- Save your maps, play them, or share them as a code or .json file. Your maps show up in New game and online.

versions.title: Online play
versions.notes:
- Play online: host a room and share the code or invite link; friends join from their browser.
- The host picks the map and options and gives each player a seat; empty seats can be AI.
- Everyone gives orders at the same time; the turn resolves once all are in. Players who drop out are replaced by AI.
- If the host leaves, you can keep playing the game on your own device against the AI.

**Limitations:** Online play needs the web version. The host's tab must stay visible: browsers pause hidden tabs.

versions.title: Groundwork for online play
versions.notes:
- Turns can now be played in lockstep between several devices: everyone sends their orders, the host gathers them and adds the AI's, and every device resolves the same turn.
- Devices compare the game state after each turn and warn if they ever disagree.

**Limitations:** No way to go online yet: the lobby comes in the next version.

versions.title: Commanders
versions.notes:
- Optional commanders (New game): one named commander per player, shown as a star in their home region.
- A commander adds +3 to battles in its region, or to an attack it goes along with (toggle it on the move).
- Take a commander's region to capture it and gain +3 armies; a commander leading a failed attack falls.
- The AI uses and hunts commanders too.

versions.title: Save and load
versions.notes:
- Five save slots plus an autosave at the start of every turn. Load game on the title screen, Save / load in the pause menu.
- Export a game as a save code to copy, or as a .json file download.
- Import by pasting a code or a .json save, or by uploading the file in the browser.

versions.title: AI opponents
versions.notes:
- AI opponents in three levels: Easy, Normal and Hard. Pick them per seat in New game.
- The AI chooses its orders at the same time as you from the public board only; it never sees your orders.
- All-AI games can be watched.

**Limitations:** Hard and Normal are close in strength, especially with random battles.

versions.title: Game options and random battles
versions.notes:
- New game screen: map, players, seats, battle mode, win share, turn limit and seed. It remembers your last choices.
- Random battles: the attacker wins with a chance of attack / (attack + defence). Deterministic battles stay the default.
- The battle log shows each attack's odds in random mode.

**Limitations:** Seats are all human until AI arrives.

versions.title: Board and animated turns
versions.notes:
- The map on screen: regions in their owner's colour with army counts.
- Give orders by tapping or dragging: deploy, move or attack, fortify, support. Reorder or delete them in the side panel.
- Two-player hotseat with a pass-the-device screen so orders stay secret.
- Orders are revealed together and play out one at a time, rotating between players, with an animated token per move. Speed and Skip buttons.
- Win screen.

**Limitations:** No AI or game options yet: Play starts a two-player hotseat game.

versions.title: Sim core and first map
versions.notes:
- The rules engine: income, orders, rotating resolution, battles, eliminations and the win check.
- First map, Iron Coast: 27 regions for 2 to 6 players.

**Limitations:** No board on screen yet: Play still opens an empty field.

versions.title: First playable
versions.notes: - Title screen, pause menu (Esc or Tab), settings, and this version log.

versions.title: More maps, smarter rivals
versions.notes:
- Map select with four boards: Greenvale (1 rival), Three Crowns (2), Four Winds (3) and Archipelago (2, islands joined by long bridges where airfields matter).
- Rival teams fight each other as well as you.
- AI difficulty: Easy, Normal or Hard (how often rivals make moves).
- Smarter AI: counts tower fire along a road or flight path, rushes help to nodes about to fall, keeps troops at its airfields for the next strike.
- How to play page on the title and pause menus.
- Sounds for sending, capturing, losing a node, tower shots, planes, upgrades, victory and defeat.
- Victory offers the next map.

versions.title: Airfields
versions.notes:
- Airfields fly troops straight to any node, ignoring roads: drag or click from your airfield to any target. Hold Shift to fly to a neighbour instead of walking.
- Each flight carries at most 15 troops and the plane needs 20 seconds to come back (the ring around the airfield fills up).
- Towers shoot planes too, so fly around enemy forts.
- The AI flies strikes at the best target its plane can take, favouring rival capitals and nodes its roads can't reach yet.
- Greenvale's bottom-middle village is now a contested airfield.

**Limitations:** One map; the AI doesn't yet weigh tower fire on the way.

versions.title: Barracks: heavy and light troops
versions.notes:
- Barracks train fewer but better troops. Select one and pick Heavy (H): slow, more than twice as strong, or Light (L): fast, a bit weaker, twice as many.
- Every unit keeps its type: a send splits into one army per type, each moving at its own speed (squares are heavy, triangles light, circles militia).
- Combat counts strength, so heavy troops break garrisons and shrug off tower fire better.
- Greenvale's top-middle village is now a contested barracks. The AI trains heavy when it borders a rival, light otherwise.

**Limitations:** No airfields yet.

versions.title: Upgrades and towers
versions.notes:
- Upgrade your villages with garrison troops: select one and press Upgrade or U. Levels 2-4 cost 10, 20 and 35 troops and raise income and the troop cap.
- Towers: forts that shoot the nearest enemy army within range, wearing big armies down and wiping out small ones. Neutral towers hold their fire until someone takes them.
- Greenvale now has a fort on each side's main road.

**Limitations:** No barracks or airfields yet; the AI doesn't upgrade (by design for now) or avoid towers.

versions.title: Board, armies and a first rival
versions.notes:
- Greenvale: a board of cities and villages joined by roads. You hold the west capital, Crimson the east.
- Owned nodes earn troops over time; neutral garrisons only defend.
- Drag from your node to a neighbour, or click your node then a target, to send troops along the road.
- Send 25/50/75/100% of the garrison: buttons at the top or keys 1-4 (50% to start).
- Armies walk the road; they reinforce your nodes and fight enemy or neutral garrisons.
- Crimson expands, attacks and pushes troops to its front. Take every rival node to win.

**Limitations:** No upgrades, towers, barracks or airfields yet; one map.

versions.title: First playable
versions.notes: - Title screen, pause menu (Esc or Tab), settings, and this version log.

versions.title: Level of the week
versions.notes:
- Level of the week: a new button on the title. Each week (from Monday) features a level made by Claude, the game's AI helper, with the same Workshop tools you have: boxes, honey, bubbles, twins, pillows and ring pins.
- The card shows the level's share code to copy, and how many treats you got this week. It plays like a shared level, so no stars toward worlds.
- Fixed: a twin level made in the Workshop (or shared as a code) now keeps Pip's treats on Pip's side.

**Limitations:** Six levels rotate for now; more can be added in later updates.

versions.title: Postcards
versions.notes:
- Postcards: finish every level of a world and Mochi sends you a postcard: that world's scenery with Mochi holding her yarn, the world's name and your stars, with a stamp. All 45 stars give it a gold border.
- It shows on the world-complete card and is kept in Extras, Postcards. Worlds you'd already finished have theirs waiting.

versions.title: Best times
versions.notes:
- Best times: every win of a world level records how long it took, and the level select shows your fastest time small under each level's number.
- The win card shows this try's time, and your best (or "fastest yet!").
- Times are kept in backup codes too; restoring keeps the faster time of each level.

**Limitations:** Times count from the moment the level starts, to the frame Mochi catches the yarn. Levels won before this update have no time until you win them again.

versions.title: Pip's trampoline
versions.notes:
- Three new bonus twin levels in the Kitchen: Pip's trampoline. A pillow both kittens share turns into a trampoline: Trampoline, Your turn, Mochi, and Bubble and bounce.
- They open after the first four bonus levels once you've beaten Pillow hop in the Kitchen, so the pillow is already familiar. The Bonus page says so.
- Bonus levels now play in their own world's look and music.

versions.title: Workshop: rails, boxes and twins
versions.notes:
- Workshop: a Rail tool (once you've met sliding pins). Tap a pin to give it a rail, drag the rail's end, and tap the end to switch between slow, medium and fast.
- Workshop: a Box tool (once you've met boxes) places a pair of linked boxes; drag each one where you like.
- Workshop: once the Bonus levels are open, Add Pip turns your level into a twin level. Switch between editing Mochi's and Pip's halves, or remove Pip again.
- Twin levels, rails and boxes all test-play and share as codes.

versions.title: Level codes v2
versions.notes:
- Level codes can now hold sliding pins on rails, cardboard box pairs and twin levels (Mochi and Pip). These use a new code (it starts PSL2-).
- Every level code shared before still works, and a level that uses none of the new things still gets the old kind of code, so friends on an older version can play it.
- A shared level with twins explains them on its card before you play.

**Limitations:** The Workshop's tools for rails, boxes and twins arrive in the next update.

versions.title: Mochi watches the yarn
versions.notes:
- Mochi watches the yarn: once you make your first move she opens her eyes and follows it (she dozes off again if you leave her alone for a while).
- A near miss makes her gasp: a little round mouth, a "!" and a soft mew.
- Each fish treat you grab gets a happy wiggle and a chirp. With Reduce motion on she keeps watching but doesn't wiggle.

versions.title: Tap to cut
versions.notes:
- New setting: Tap to cut. Turn it on and a tap on a rope snips it, for anyone who finds swiping hard. Swipes still work, and a tap on a bubble, fan or spool still does what it always did.
- With it on, the first level's hint and the How to play Snip card say to tap.

versions.title: Cardboard City complete
versions.notes:
- Cardboard City is complete with 15 levels: new are Blown off course (a fan starts the swing), Relay (three boxes in a row), Handle with care (box, honey and a cactus) and the finale.
- Box levels now turn up in the daily puzzle too.
- How to play has a Boxes card, the Sticker book has Cardboard City and Cardboard feast stickers, and Cardboard City has its own take on the lullaby with soft woodblock taps.

versions.title: Cardboard City, levels 8-11
versions.notes:
- Four more Cardboard City levels: Sticky parcel (honey after the box), Conveyor (a sliding pin carries the yarn over the box), Signed for (a ring pin catches the yarn as it pops out) and Wind and post (wind the spool, swing, then drop it in the box).

**Limitations:** Cardboard City has 11 of its 15 levels so far.

versions.title: Cardboard City, levels 4-7
versions.notes:
- Four more Cardboard City levels: Two pairs (paw goes to paw, star goes to star), Box spring (out of a box onto a pillow), Air mail (a bubble carries the yarn up into a box, so pop it at the right moment) and Fragile (skip the cactus by dropping the yarn into a box).

**Limitations:** Cardboard City has 7 of its 15 levels so far.

versions.title: Cardboard City and box portals
versions.notes:
- World 5, Cardboard City, opens at 120 stars: a paper-sky town of cardboard box buildings.
- New: cardboard box portals. Boxes come in linked pairs (told apart by a stamp on the label: a paw or a star). A loose yarn that drops into one pops out of its twin with the same speed and direction.
- Boxes only take a yarn no rope is holding: their flaps stay closed until it's free. A pair that has been used six times in one try gets taped shut.
- The first three box levels: Special delivery (a gentle lesson with a hint), Return to sender and Out the side.

**Limitations:** Cardboard City has 3 of its 15 levels so far; more arrive in the next updates. Box levels aren't in the daily puzzle yet.

versions.title: Performance pass
versions.notes:
- Smoother on phones: each world's backdrop is now drawn once instead of every frame (the Rooftop's stars still twinkle).
- Cactus pots and honey blobs are drawn with far fewer pieces: about a third fewer draw calls on the busiest levels.
- Faster start: sounds are made in the background after the title appears instead of all at once while loading.

versions.title: Performance overlay
versions.notes:
- A performance overlay: press F3 (or add ?perf=1 to the page address on a phone) to see frames per second, frame times, how long the game's drawing and physics take, and draw calls. It also writes a PERF line to the browser console every 5 seconds.
- The console gets one PERF startup line with how long the game took to start.
- Behind the scenes: a bench script times every level's physics and the busiest screens, so the next update's speed-ups can be measured.

**Limitations:** Measuring only; the speed-ups come in the next update.

versions.title: New-player check
versions.notes:
- Behind the scenes: a new automatic check plays the game the way a brand-new player meets it: an empty save, the title, the first level won with a real swipe, the result card, Continue, the level select, then World 1 in order until the Garden opens at 30 stars.
- Nothing changes in play; this guards the first minutes of the game against quiet breakage.

versions.title: Back up progress
versions.notes:
- Settings, Back up progress: copy your save as a code (stars, bonus stars, stickers, dailies and outfit) to keep it safe or move it to another device.
- Restore by pasting a backup code. The game checks it, tells you what it holds, and asks first. Restoring keeps the best of both saves, so nothing is ever lost, and your old save is kept as a copy too.
- A wrong or cut-off code just gets a friendly note.

versions.title: Daily calendar
versions.notes:
- The daily puzzle card (and its result card) shows your last week: the stars you got each day, a cross for a day you tried but didn't win, a dash for a day you missed, and today outlined.
- Under it: how many dailies you won this week and in all. Past days can't be replayed, so streaks stay honest.

versions.title: Twin levels
versions.notes:
- Bonus twin levels: two yarns and two kittens, Mochi and her friend Pip (a ginger tabby on a striped cushion, with striped blue yarn). Every swipe snips both sides, and the level is won when both kittens have their yarn.
- Four of them, under a new Bonus tab in the level select, open once you've finished the Living Room. The first one teaches the idea with a hint and can't be lost.
- Bonus stars are just for fun: they don't count toward world gates or the wardrobe. Finishing them all earns the Twin tamer sticker, and How to play has a Twins card.

versions.title: Share codes
versions.notes:
- Share your workshop levels: once you've beaten a level, Share shows a short code (like PSL1-...) to copy and send.
- Workshop, Play a code: paste a friend's code (or use Paste) and play it. Codes forgive lower case, spaces and an O typed for a zero. A wrong, cut-off or newer code just gets a friendly note, and nothing you have is changed.
- If a shared level has gadgets you haven't met yet, a card explains them first. You can save a shared level to your own levels.
- New sticker: Level maker, for sharing a level.

versions.title: Level workshop
versions.notes:
- A Workshop in Extras: build your own levels. Place the yarn, pins, three treats, Mochi, and any gadget you've met (cactus, bubble, fan, honey, ring pin, pillow); drag to move; tap a pin again for slack or a spool, a fan to turn it, a pillow to tilt it.
- Test plays your level for real; beating it marks it beaten. Up to 12 levels are saved on this device.
- Your levels give no stars, and everything snaps to a tidy grid and stays where it can be played.

versions.title: Sticker book
versions.notes:
- A Sticker book in Extras: 13 stickers for milestones, like your first 3-treat level, finishing each world, finding every treat in a world, winning daily puzzles (first win, 3 days in a row, 7 wins) and 100 stars.
- Win cards say when you earn one. Stickers you'd already earned before this update are handed out the first time you open the game.
- Locked stickers show how to earn them.

versions.title: How to play, and Extras
versions.notes:
- A How to play page (Extras on the title): a card for snipping, treats and every gadget, each with a tiny looping demo of the level that teaches it and a pointer showing the swipe, tap or hold.
- Cards open as you reach their teaching level, so nothing is spoiled; the rest say which world they're in.
- The title's Wardrobe button moved into Extras.

versions.title: Music for every world
versions.notes:
- Each world now has its own take on the lullaby: the Living Room as before, birdsong over a brighter Garden, a slower, lower Rooftop at night, and a brisker Kitchen with a soft plucked bass.
- A world's tune is made the first time you play there (the last one keeps playing meanwhile), then crossfades in over two seconds. The daily puzzle plays its world's tune.

versions.title: Kitchen complete
versions.notes:
- The Kitchen's last five levels: Rail bounce, Pillow relay (three pillows), Bubble trouble, Sticky rail and the Kitchen finale (wind, drop, bounce and a ring pin).
- World 4 is ordered gentle to hard like the others, and finishing it shows the all-worlds card.
- 60 levels in all, 180 stars to collect.

versions.title: Kitchen levels 6-10
versions.notes:
- Five more Kitchen levels that mix pillows with what you know: Fan bounce, Prickly pillow, Honey landing (honey softens a big bounce), Wind and drop (a spool) and Ring bounce (a ring pin catches the yarn after a hop).
- Each one gives at least 4 ticks of leeway either way on every snip, puff and hold.

**Limitations:** World 4 has 10 of its 15 levels so far.

versions.title: World 4: the Kitchen, and bouncy pillows
versions.notes:
- World 4, the Kitchen, opens at 90 stars: mint tiles, a wooden counter, and its first five levels.
- New: bouncy pillows. The yarn bounces off them (the rope's loose tail bounces too) and they squash with a soft pomf. Pillow hop teaches them with a hint before any pillow can make you miss.
- Pillows have a dark outline, a stitched seam and little springs, so they read without colour, and every pillow is tilted so the yarn never gets stuck bouncing on one.
- Kitchen levels can turn up in the daily puzzle, and its card explains pillows.

**Limitations:** World 4 has 5 of its 15 levels so far.

versions.title: Gentle to hard, and treats left
versions.notes:
- Each world now plays from gentle to hard: levels were ordered by how many moves and tricks they need and how much timing leeway they give. Each world's first level and finale stay put, and every new trick still comes with its teaching level first.
- Your stars carry over: they belong to the level, not its number, and any level you've already beaten stays open.
- In the level select, a beaten level with treats still to find shows a little fish badge with how many are left, and the page counts them. Under a locked world it says how many stars you still need.
- Continue on the title now says which world and level, like World 2 · Level 3.

versions.title: Difficulty pass
versions.notes:
- Every level was measured for timing leeway: how many ticks early or late each snip, tap and hold can be and still win with all three treats.
- The early Living Room levels are now more forgiving: Two ropes, Big swing, Up high and Timing give at least 4 ticks either way (Mochi or a treat moved slightly), and Three ropes cuts later at a gentler moment.
- Balloon breeze's second puff and Ring ladder's middle snip got more room, so every level now allows at least 3 ticks either way on every action.

versions.title: Daily puzzle
versions.notes:
- A Daily puzzle on the title screen: one level a day, the same for everyone, picked from levels across all three worlds (mirrored on odd days for a fresh look). It's open from the start, and a card before it explains every trick in it.
- Your daily result counts treats, tries and a streak of days in a row, and Copy result copies a short text to share, like: [*][*][ ] 2 of 3 treats, 3 tries. Daily stars don't change your level stars.
- Copying needs the browser's clipboard permission; the result text is also shown so you can select it.

versions.title: Mochi's wardrobe
versions.notes:
- A Wardrobe on the title screen: dress Mochi in a hat and a collar. Six outfits unlock with total stars: bell collar (10), beanie (25), bow tie (45), flower crown (65), scarf (90) and a starry nightcap (115).
- The win card tells you when a new outfit unlocks. Your pick is saved and Mochi wears it in every level.

versions.title: Calm mode
versions.notes:
- Settings has a Reduce motion switch: no confetti, squash, hopping, bobbing treats, wobbly bubbles or shivering ropes, steady glows instead of pulses, and stars that appear without bursting. Mochi's slow naps stay.
- Cactus pots always show their snag zone as a dashed ring of little spikes, so the danger reads by shape, not just colour.

versions.title: Phone friendly
versions.notes:
- On-screen Pause and Retry buttons in the top corner while you play, so phones can pause and retry too.
- On phones the menus, level select and sliders scale up to thumb size, and a menu too tall for a sideways phone scrolls.
- Long hints wrap onto two lines and the hint text is a little bigger.
- Swipes no longer scroll, zoom or select the page, and a long press brings up no menu; a held spool lets go if your finger leaves the page.

versions.title: Lullaby
versions.notes:
- Soft background music: a music-box lullaby over a warm pad, made in code (no audio files). It fades in a moment after the game starts.
- Settings now have separate Music and Sounds volumes (your old volume becomes the Sounds volume). The unused mouse sensitivity setting is gone.
- Ropes creak softly and shiver when they pull taut, and when a spool hauls the yarn up.

versions.title: Rooftop, complete
versions.notes:
- The Rooftop now has all 15 levels: a spool duet, a spool that rides a rail, a ring ladder, Moonbeam, and the Grand rooftop finale.
- Finishing the Rooftop shows a card for finishing every world. 45 levels in all.

versions.title: Rooftop, part 2
versions.notes:
- Five more Rooftop levels (6-10) with four tricks each and more steps: a ring relay, a balloon blown across the sky, a moonlit bubble rail, a hop from one bubble to the next, and a rail that hands the yarn to a ring.
- The Rooftop has 10 of its 15 levels so far.

versions.title: Rooftop at night
versions.notes:
- World 3, the Rooftop at night, opens at 60 stars: a starry sky, a moon, and rooftops with lit windows.
- The first five Rooftop levels mix three things each: bubbles and fans by a cactus, a moonlit ring with honey, a chimney bubble on a rail, a gusty spool, and a night rail.
- The ghost path is lighter on the night sky.
- The Rooftop has 5 of its 15 levels so far.

versions.title: Garden, complete
versions.notes:
- The Garden now has all 15 levels: a honey rail, a bubble reeled in on a spool, two spools at once, a prickly breeze, and the Garden finale.
- Finishing the Garden shows a World 2 complete card.

versions.title: Garden, part 2
versions.notes: - Five more Garden levels (6-10): float a bubble over honey, keep a short spool rope clear of a cactus, blow the yarn into honey with a fan, wind up into a ring's reach, and wind a wild swing into honey to calm it.

versions.title: The Garden
versions.notes:
- World 2, the Garden, opens at 30 stars: a sunny backdrop with a hedge, a picket fence and flowers.
- Sticky honey: the yarn oozes slowly through a honey blob, a handy brake.
- Spinning spools: press and hold a spool to wind its rope in; let go to stop.
- Five new levels so far (Garden 1-5), each new thing with its own lesson first.
- Level select has a tab per world; levels are numbered per world, and finishing a world says what the next one needs.
- The first 5 of the Garden's 15 levels; more in the next updates.

versions.title: Level check-up
versions.notes:
- Behind the scenes: every level is now played automatically on each build, checking its solution wins with all three fish treats and still works a couple of ticks early or late.
- No gameplay changes.

versions.title: Sleepy Mochi
versions.notes:
- Mochi flicks her tail, twitches an ear and has a long stretch while she naps, on the title screen too.
- Take more than 20 seconds without a snip and she yawns.

versions.title: Ghost path
versions.notes:
- On a retry, a faint dotted ghost shows the yarn's path from your last attempt, with rings where you cut or tapped.
- It's cleared when you change level or go back to the menu, and a retry without a snip keeps the old one.

versions.title: A helping paw
versions.notes:
- After three tries on a level, the first rope to snip (or fan or bubble to tap) glows, with a small banner. It fades once you act and comes back on each retry until you win.
- Restarting before you've cut or tapped anything doesn't count as a try.

versions.title: Snip feel
versions.notes:
- Cut rope ends flick back and wiggle, with a little puff of fibre.
- The swipe leaves a tapered glowing ribbon with a bright tip.
- Softer snip sounds in three pitches.

versions.title: Sliding pins
versions.notes:
- Sliding pins: a pin that glides along a rail, so when you snip matters.
- Level 14, Sliding pin: snip when the yarn is over Mochi. Level 15, Grand finale: a slide, a swing and a cactus.
- World 1 now has 15 levels, and finishing it shows a World 1 complete card with your stars.

versions.title: Cactus pots
versions.notes:
- Cactus pots: the first hazard. If the yarn touches one it snags and unravels, and the level is lost.
- Spines bristle and glow when the yarn gets close, as a warning.
- Level 13, Prickly pot: a familiar two-rope puzzle where the wrong snip order swings into a cactus.
- The lose card says when the yarn snagged.

versions.title: Ring pins
versions.notes:
- Ring pins: a dotted ring that ties a new rope to the yarn as it passes, once.
- Level 12, Ring catch: drop into the ring, then snip the new rope over Mochi.
- Hints now sit under the ropes and pins, so they never hide a pin.

versions.title: Happy catch
versions.notes:
- Mochi catches the yarn with a squash-and-stretch bounce, and a burst of yarn scraps and hearts.
- The yarn eases into her paws instead of stopping at the edge.
- Stars on the win card pop in one at a time, each with a rising chime; a new best gets a little star burst.

versions.title: Level select
versions.notes:
- Level select: every level with its best stars; a level opens once the one before is beaten.
- Continue on the title screen picks up at the last level you played (or the next one after a win).
- Levels in the pause menu too, and a World 2 star gate (coming soon).
- Bubbles now shake off the loose tail of a cut rope, so a floating yarn never looks tied to its pin.

versions.title: Air puffers
versions.notes:
- Little desk fans: tap one to blow the yarn (or its bubble) sideways.
- Level 10, Fan club: puff, then snip as it swings to Mochi. Level 11, Breezy bubble: blow a bubble over Mochi, then pop.
- Fan whoosh sound; breeze lines show where a fan blows.

versions.title: Bubbles
versions.notes:
- Bubbles: the yarn floats up inside one until you tap to pop it.
- Level 8, Bubble lift: a gentle bubble lesson. Level 9, Balloon ride: snip it free over Mochi, then pop.
- A tap on a bubble never starts a swipe; the bubble hint stays up until your first pop.
- Bubble and pop sounds.

versions.title: Title nap
versions.notes:
- Mochi naps behind the title menu.
- Fixed: the level counter ran off the right edge of the playfield.

versions.title: Tutorial levels
versions.notes:
- Seven short levels, each teaching one idea: one snip, cut order, a big swing, treats up high, three ropes, timing, and a slack rope.
- A one-line hint at the start of each level, and a level counter at the top.
- Play picks up at the first level you haven't beaten; the title shows your stars.
- After the last level, a 'more soon' card.

**Limitations:** Seven levels for now; more puzzles and new gadgets to come.

versions.title: Fish treats and stars
versions.notes:
- Three fish treats float in each level; swing the yarn through one to collect it (with a sparkle).
- The win card shows 0-3 stars, one per treat, and says when it's a new best.
- Your best stars per level are saved.
- Collected treats show at the top of the playfield.

**Limitations:** Still the one test level; the tutorial levels come next.

versions.title: Meet Mochi
versions.notes:
- Mochi the kitten naps on her cushion; she wakes, watches and reaches as the yarn gets close.
- Drop the yarn into her paws to win (hearts and a purr). Let it fall past her and it's a miss.
- Result card with Next, Retry and Menu; press R to retry any time.
- Little sounds made in code: snip, bump, purr, miss.

**Limitations:** Only the one test level so far.
